opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things that surprised us too when we first started doing these interventions.

So the setup, for listeners, is something like the poetry example: the model is writing a rhyming couplet, and before it even starts the second line, it's already sort of planning ahead. It has picked a word it wants to land on, like "rabbit," and you can see features representing that planned word light up. Then we go in and suppress that feature, or swap in a different one, and the model writes a completely different line that ends somewhere else.

The puzzle you're pointing at is: if the representation of "rabbit" isn't sitting in one spot, if it's smeared across many layers and many token positions, why would poking it in one place be enough?

The way I think about it is that a concept being *present* across many layers isn't the same as every one of those copies being equally *causal* for a given behavior. The residual stream is this shared channel that every layer reads from and writes to. When a feature gets written at some layer, later layers pick it up, maybe refine it, maybe copy it forward, maybe use it to compute something else. So a lot of what looks like "the rabbit concept in layers 15, 16, 17, 18" is really a chain where the later appearances depend on the earlier ones. If you intervene early enough in that chain, the downstream copies never get formed in the first place, or they get formed around whatever you substituted in.

Another piece is that these features often have pretty specific roles. There's a difference between "the model is representing that rabbit was mentioned" and "the model is using rabbit as a target to steer toward." The planning features we're intervening on are the ones that downstream computation actually reads when it's deciding how to construct the line. You don't have to wipe out every trace of the word. You just have to change the thing the later layers are consulting.

And to be honest, it doesn't always work cleanly. Sometimes you intervene at one layer and the model kind of recovers, because there's redundancy, some other pathway reconstructs the information. That's actually informative too. When a single-layer intervention works, that tells you something about where the bottleneck is. When it doesn't, it tells you the computation is more distributed and you need to intervene across several layers at once, which is something we do with things like cross-layer transcoders, where a feature can write to many layers at once and you can manipulate it as a unit.

So the short version: distributed representation doesn't mean distributed control. There are usually points where the information funnels through, and if you find those, a fairly local edit can have a really global effect on what the model ends up saying.

r001.rationale: The response explains that an early single-layer intervention can change later appearances of the rabbit representation because subsequent layers pick it up, refine it, or copy it forward. It does not say “first layer” explicitly, but it conveys the same causal propagation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question we got a lot when we put out the planning-in-poems result, and I think it's a really good one, because it does feel paradoxical at first. We say the model is representing "rabbit" as a planned word, and when you go look, that feature is active across a bunch of layers, not just one. So how can an intervention at a single layer do anything?

The way I think about it is that the residual stream in a transformer is basically a running tally. Each layer reads from it and writes back into it, and what the next layer sees is the sum of everything that came before. So when we say the rabbit concept is "spread across layers," what we really mean is that multiple layers are contributing to it, and it's accumulating. It's not that there are five independent copies of rabbit living in five separate places that you'd have to hunt down one by one.

Now, when we intervene at one layer, say we subtract out the rabbit direction and add in the "green" direction, or whatever we're swapping to, we're changing what gets passed downstream. Everything after that point is reading a modified residual stream. And a lot of the later layers aren't independently recomputing "rabbit" from scratch. They're reading the signal that's already there and often amplifying it or acting on it. If you've knocked it out before they get to it, they just don't see it, and so they don't reinforce it, and the model goes and plans around the new word instead.

There's a caveat, which is that this doesn't always work perfectly. Sometimes an upstream layer that we didn't touch will have already written rabbit, and we only intervened downstream, and in those cases the effect can be partial, or the model partially recovers. Where you intervene matters a lot. In practice we found that intervening around the middle of the network, kind of where the planning features first get written strongly, was most effective. And when it worked, it was pretty striking: the model would write a line that rhymed with the new word, and the line would make sense in context, which tells you it wasn't just a one-token hack, it actually rerouted the plan.

So I'd say the resolution to the paradox is that "spread across layers" and "causally dependent on one point in the stream" aren't in tension. The concept can be distributed in the sense of being contributed to and used by many layers, while still having a bottleneck where a single edit propagates through the whole computation. Honestly, that's one of the reasons interventions are so useful to us, because they let you distinguish between "this feature correlates with rabbit" and "the model is actually using this to decide what to say."

r001.rationale: The response says a single-layer intervention can affect downstream layers because they may amplify the signal, but it does not say that changing the first layer can do so. It instead highlights interventions around the middle of the network.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is that a concept being distributed across layers doesn’t mean each layer has an independent copy of it. The layers interact. So if you change how one layer processes information related to rabbits, that changes what the subsequent layers receive and, potentially, what the model ultimately does.

You don’t need to find a single place where the entire rabbit concept lives to influence it. But influencing the model’s behavior around rabbits also doesn’t establish that you’ve changed every aspect of that concept. You might affect one association or one way it gets expressed while leaving others intact.

r001.rationale: The response says changing one layer can affect what subsequent layers receive and the model’s behavior, but it does not identify the first layer or explain that later layers amplify the representation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a concept being distributed across layers doesn’t mean that each layer has an independent copy of it. These layers are building on each other. So if you change how one layer represents or processes something related to rabbits, you’re also changing the information that the downstream layers receive.

You can think of it as intervening at one point in a computation. You don’t need to change every step of that computation to change its result. That helps explain how an intervention in one layer can affect the model’s behavior around rabbits, even though the concept itself isn’t localized to that layer.

r001.rationale: The response explains that changing one layer alters the information downstream layers receive, but it does not say that subsequent layers amplify the representation.
